summary: The root شَكَّ (shakka) primarily means to doubt or be uncertain about something. It implies a state of hesitation or wavering belief, often due to a lack of clear evidence or conviction.

provenance.lane: Edward William Lane, An Arabic-English Lexicon (1863-93), public domain. Digital text via Perseus, Tufts University, CC BY-SA 3.0 US.
provenance.summary: Editorial summary derived from the Lane entry. NOT Lane's own wording. Shown as a gloss only; the Lane text below is the source.

headwords.def: مِشَكٌّ The thong with which the coat of mail is [ in certain parts thereof ] conjoined ( يُشَكُّ بِهِ ): 'Antarah says, وَمِشَكِّ سَابِغَةٍ هَتَكْتُ فُرُوجَهَا بِالسَّيْفِ عَنْ حَامِى الحَقِيقَةِ مُعْلَمِ (O, TA:) [but in the EM it is مَسَكِّ , thus with س , and with fet-h to the م ; a word which I do not find in any lexicon: it is said that] مسك signifies a coat of mail narrow in the rings: and the poet means, And of many an ample coat of mail [ narrow in the rings ] have I rent open the middle parts with the sword, from over a man who was the defender of those who, or that which, it was his duty to defend, who was pointed to as being the cavalier of the army. (EM p. 243.)
